description: The tomato foliage exhibits vibrant green coloration, uniform leaf blade architecture, and no visible fungal, bacterial, or necrotic lesions.
symptoms: Lush, uniform green leaf coloration
Intact vein structure without interveinal chlorosis
Absence of concentric ring spots or water-soaked lesions
Sturdy petiole and vigorous vegetative growth
causes: Balanced soil nutrients (adequate N-P-K and calcium)
Optimal irrigation schedule avoiding leaf wetness
Good air circulation and full sun exposure
prevention: Maintain consistent drip irrigation at the root zone
Mulch soil to prevent rain-splash from soil pathogens
Prune lower foliage that contacts soil
Practice 3-4 year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops
management: Continue routine weekly scouting
Ensure staking or caging allows 50cm+ spacing between plants
Sanitize pruning tools with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows
warning: Healthy foliage should continue to be monitored weekly, particularly following heavy precipitation or high humidity spells.

description: Early blight is a common fungal disease characterized by brown-to-black necrotic lesions exhibiting a distinctive concentric ring or 'bullseye' pattern, typically starting on older, lower leaves.
symptoms: Circular brown spots with characteristic concentric rings (target-board appearance)
Chlorotic yellow halos encircling the necrotic lesions
Premature yellowing and defoliation progressing upward from lower canopy
Sunscald risk on developing fruit due to lost leaf cover
causes: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani surviving in plant debris or solanaceous weeds
Prolonged leaf wetness combined with warm temperatures (24-29°C / 75-85°F)
Rain splash spreading fungal spores from soil to lower foliage
Stressed or nutrient-depleted plants
prevention: Apply organic or plastic mulch around the base of plants to block spore splash
Water exclusively at soil level using drip or soaker hoses; avoid overhead sprinklers
Provide wide plant spacing (60-90 cm) for maximum airflow and rapid canopy drying
Rotate crops on a 3-year cycle away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplants
Plant certified disease-tolerant or resistant cultivars (e.g., Mountain Supreme, Defiant)
management: Immediately prune off severely affected lower leaves during dry weather and bag them; do NOT compost infected leaves
Stake and cage plants to elevate all foliage off the ground
Apply protective preventive bio-fungicides (such as Bacillus subtilis or copper hydroxide) according to local extension labels when conditions favor infection
Clear and destroy all crop residues at the conclusion of the growing season
warning: Always follow local agricultural extension guidelines. This diagnostic system is an informational decision-support tool and does not replace on-field laboratory verification.
sources: UC IPM Pest Management Guidelines - Tomato Early Blight

description: Late blight is an aggressive oomycete pathogen capable of devastating tomato and potato canopies within days during cool, humid, and rainy weather. Produces irregular water-soaked pale-to-dark olive lesions.
symptoms: Irregular, water-soaked, dark-green to purplish-brown lesions on leaves and petioles
Delicate white fuzzy fungal-like sporulation on the underside of leaves during high humidity
Rapid collapse, browning, and shriveling of entire leaf branches
Brown greasy-looking firm rot patches on developing green or ripe tomatoes
causes: Oomycete organism Phytophthora infestans transported by windborne sporangia
Cool to moderate temperatures (15-22°C / 60-72°F) accompanied by relative humidity above 85%
Extended morning dew or frequent rainfall keeping foliage wet for 10+ hours
prevention: Inspect transplants carefully and plant only certified disease-free seedlings
Eliminate volunteer potato and tomato plants within 1 km of production fields
Select resistant tomato cultivars (e.g., Mountain Magic, Iron Lady, Plum Regal)
Avoid overhead irrigation entirely; ensure optimal solar orientation for rapid morning dry-off
management: Immediately isolate infected zones and rogue out heavily infected plants in plastic bags to stop airborne spore release
Alert neighboring growers as late blight spores can disperse miles on wind currents
If caught at the earliest stage, apply approved copper-based protectant sprays under the supervision of a licensed agronomist
Ensure no cull piles or infected tubers are left exposed in the field
warning: Late blight spreads rapidly and can cause 100% crop loss if left unmanaged. Notify regional agricultural extension officers upon confirmed detection.
sources: FAO Plant Production and Protection Guidelines
University of Florida IFAS Extension - Tomato Late Blight

description: Vigorous potato foliage with rich dark green leaflets, balanced canopy density, and no necrotic speckling or chlorosis.
symptoms: Crisp, uniform green leaflets with well-defined margins
Healthy upright stems without dark streaking
Vigorous tuber-initiation foliage without curling or spotting
causes: Certified clean seed tubers planted in well-drained, acidic soil (pH 5.0-6.0)
Adequate soil hilling protecting tubers and roots
Controlled moisture without waterlogging
prevention: Plant certified seed potatoes only
Maintain adequate hilling to protect tubers from light and soil pathogens
Maintain optimal nitrogen levels (excessive nitrogen promotes overly lush, susceptible foliage)
management: Perform regular field transect walks to inspect lower canopies
Keep field borders clean of wild nightshade weeds
warning: Maintain consistent scouting, particularly during tuber bulking stages.

description: Fungal disease in potatoes causing dark brown angular or circular spots on foliage with concentric ridges. Accelerates foliage senescence and reduces tuber yield.
symptoms: Dark brown to black circular lesions on older leaflets with concentric rings
Yellowing tissue surrounding lesion borders that coalesces as infection spreads
Dry, papery texture of severely infected leaves that remain hanging on the vine
Dark, sunken, leathery lesions on harvested tubers with raised margins
causes: Alternaria solani spores overwintering in previous potato vine residue
Cycles of wet conditions followed by warm dry winds promoting spore release
Physiologically aging or potassium-deficient potato plants
prevention: Provide balanced crop nutrition with adequate potassium and split nitrogen applications
Utilize long rotations (at least 3 to 4 years) away from potato, tomato, and eggplant
Schedule irrigation early in the morning so potato vines dry completely before midday
Choose medium-to-late maturing varieties that demonstrate higher field tolerance
management: Remove diseased vines prior to harvest or vine-kill effectively to prevent spore transfer to tubers
Apply protective botanical or chemical treatments registered for potato early blight at row closure
Allow tubers to mature in the ground for 10-14 days after vine desiccation to thicken skin before harvesting
warning: Do not harvest when soil is wet as soil abrasions can introduce Alternaria spores into potato tubers.
sources: North Dakota State University Extension - Potato Early Blight

description: The notorious pathogen responsible for the Irish Potato Famine. Attacks both potato foliage and tubers with rapid necrosis under cool, wet climatic conditions.
symptoms: Pale green water-soaked spots enlarging rapidly into large dark brown or purplish-black lesions
White mildew-like sporulation visible on the undersides of leaves during damp conditions
Stems show dark brown greasy lesions that cause stems to snap easily
Tubers exhibit dry, granular, reddish-brown rot spreading from the surface inwards
causes: Infected seed tubers planted in spring or unharvested cull potatoes in nearby dumps
Continuous foliage wetness for >8 hours under temperatures of 12-24°C (53-75°F)
High relative humidity (>90%) facilitating rapid sporulation
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed tubers with zero late blight tolerance
Destroy all cull piles by burying under at least 2 feet of soil or covering with black plastic
Plant tolerant varieties (e.g., Sarpo Mira, Defender, Elba)
Avoid poorly drained sections of the field where moisture pools
management: Destroy localized infection hot spots immediately by flaming or desiccating plants within a 5-meter radius
Apply approved protective fungicides prior to canopy closure when disease warning models indicate high risk
Ensure vines are 100% dead for a minimum of 2 weeks before harvest to prevent tuber contamination
warning: Immediate containment is imperative. Late blight can destroy an entire field within 7 to 10 days.

description: Healthy maize foliage featuring robust, elongated linear leaves with clean margins, prominent central midrib, and no rust pustules or elongated blights.
symptoms: Even green coloration across entire leaf blade
Clear midrib and absence of powdery pustules
Unrestricted leaf photosynthetic area supporting ear development
causes: Optimal soil pH (6.0-6.8) and balanced nitrogen fertilization
Adequate soil drainage and appropriate plant population density
Good weed competition suppression
prevention: Follow regional soil-test nitrogen and phosphorus recommendations
Maintain 75 cm row spacing to optimize sunlight penetration and air movement
Rotate fields with legumes (soybeans/alfalfa) to replenish soil health
management: Scout fields at V6 (six-leaf collar) and VT (tasseling) stages
Keep field records of hybrid performance
warning: Continue regular scouting throughout the silking and grain filling periods.
sources: Purdue University Extension - Corn Field Guide

description: Fungal infection causing small, circular-to-elongate golden-brown to cinnamon-brown pustules scattered across both the upper and lower leaf surfaces of maize.
symptoms: Small, elevated, oval pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the leaf epidermis, releasing powdery cinnamon-brown urediniospores
Chlorotic ring often forms around clusters of pustules
Severe infection causes premature leaf yellowing and dieback
causes: Puccinia sorghi fungal spores carried on southerly winds from tropical/subtropical zones
Cool to moderate temperatures (16-25°C / 60-77°F) with high relative humidity (>95%)
Free moisture on leaves from overnight dew lasting 6-8 hours
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant corn hybrids with Rp-resistance genes
Plant early in the season so grain fill occurs prior to peak spore migration
Avoid planting susceptible sweet corn varieties directly downwind of early field corn
management: Scout mid-canopy leaves before tasseling (V8 to VT); evaluate rust severity on the ear leaf
If pustules cover >10% of ear leaf area before blister (R2) stage and conditions favor spread, consult an agronomist for targeted foliar treatment
Hot and dry weather (>30°C / 86°F) naturally suppresses rust development
warning: Common rust is typically less devastating than Southern Rust, but sweet corn and inbred seed lines require proactive monitoring.
sources: University of Illinois Extension - Corn Diseases
Purdue Extension - Common Rust of Corn

description: A destructive fungal foliar disease of maize producing characteristic long, elliptical, cigar-shaped grayish-green to tan lesions.
symptoms: Elongated, elliptical lesions (2.5 to 15 cm long) shaped like cigars
Initial lesions appear grayish-green, turning tan as tissue becomes necrotic
Dark olive or black fungal spores visible in the center of lesions under humid conditions
Multiple lesions coalesce, causing extensive blighting of entire leaf blades
causes: Exserohilum turcicum fungus overwintering on infested corn residue on the soil surface
Moderate temperatures (18-27°C / 65-80°F) accompanied by extended periods of wet weather (6-18 hours dew/rain)
Continuous no-till or minimum-till corn-on-corn cropping systems
prevention: Select corn hybrids containing Ht-resistance genes (Ht1, Ht2, Ht3, or polygenic resistance)
Rotate to non-host crops such as soybeans, wheat, or legumes for at least one to two years
Tillage management: Incorporate crop debris into the soil where residue-dwelling fungi decompose faster
Ensure balanced soil potassium as low potassium levels increase susceptibility
management: Scout leaves below the ear before tasseling and monitor progression onto the ear leaf
Prioritize management if disease reaches the ear leaf or higher before R2 (blister) stage
Foliar protectants can be considered in high-yield commercial fields if threshold is reached on susceptible hybrids
warning: Severe infection before or during pollination can lead to grain yield losses exceeding 30-50% due to loss of photosynthetic canopy.
sources: Iowa State University Crop Protection Network - Northern Corn Leaf Blight
